Coach's notebook, college cricket, 18 November
Talked with Hemant after nets today. Last month Nikhil told the selectors Hemant had skipped training, which wasn't true, and Hemant lost his place. Hemant has barely spoken to him since.
Today Hemant said something new. He had overheard Nikhil on the phone with his father, being shouted at about the sports scholarship. 'He was scared, Coach. He'd lose the fees if he got dropped.'
Then he added quickly, 'It's still not okay, what he did.'
I agreed with both parts. Understanding why doesn't make it right.
He seemed looser in the shoulders than he has in weeks, and bowled well.
Next step: I'll raise the false report with the selectors myself, and ask Hemant if he wants me there when he talks to Nikhil.
- Raghav

qa.q: What false thing did Nikhil tell the selectors?
qa.a: Nikhil told them Hemant had skipped training.

qa.q: What does Hemant's quick 'It's still not okay' show?
qa.a: It shows he understands Nikhil's fear without excusing the lie, holding both at once.

qa.q: What does Raghav plan next, and why is it fair?
qa.a: Raghav will raise the false report with the selectors and offer to be there if Hemant talks to Nikhil, so understanding doesn't mean the wrong goes unaddressed.

qa.q: What might Nikhil have been experiencing when his father shouted about the scholarship?
qa.a: Nikhil was likely frightened of losing his fees and under heavy pressure, which may have pushed him into the lie.

passage:
Sunday night
Gurleen's cousin told me today why she didn't turn up for my college interview in May, after promising to drive me. I waited at the gate for forty minutes and missed my slot. I've hated her since.
Turns out that morning her dad was taken to hospital, and she was so ashamed of the scene at home she couldn't tell anyone. Not even me.
I sat on the steps for a long time after hearing that.
I'm still angry. She could have sent one text. That's true and I'm not pretending it isn't.
But I can see her now: panicking, embarrassed, nineteen, with no good choices. She's not the villain I built up in my head. She's a person who messed up on the worst day of her life.
It's weird. The bitterness feels looser. Not gone.
- Kishore

qa.q: How long did Kishore wait at the gate?
qa.a: Kishore waited at the gate for forty minutes.

qa.q: How does Kishore feel after hearing what happened to Gurleen?
qa.a: Still angry that one text was never sent, but the bitterness has loosened as Kishore understands her panic and shame.

qa.q: Why doesn't understanding mean Kishore has to excuse Gurleen?
qa.a: Kishore can see why she failed to turn up while still holding that she could have sent a text; understanding eases bitterness without approving the act.

qa.q: What might Gurleen have been going through that morning?
qa.a: She was likely panicking about her dad and ashamed of the scene at home, feeling unable to tell anyone.

grounding: It shows someone coming to understand a friend's panic and shame on a hard day without excusing the broken promise, and feeling bitterness loosen.

The Howrah express was four hours late, and the only empty seat in the crowded sleeper coach was opposite Gopika, the college friend who had spread the rumour that cost Abhinav his place as student secretary last year.
They sat in stiff silence for two hours. Then, somewhere past Asansol, with the lights flickering, Gopika spoke. "I was scared that year. My scholarship depended on the student council's recommendation, and the other group promised me theirs if I helped them. I told myself the rumour was half true."
Abhinav wanted to say, that's no excuse. It wasn't. But he watched her twist the strap of her bag, and remembered her mother was a cook at the hostel, and that the scholarship was everything.
"It was still wrong," he said.
"I know," she said. "I've known for a year."
He didn't forgive her on the train. But as they reached Howrah in the grey dawn, the bitterness he had carried felt a little less heavy.

qa.q: What did the rumour cost Abhinav?
qa.a: His place as student secretary last year.

qa.q: What does Abhinav feel watching Gopika twist her bag strap?
qa.a: He feels a reluctant understanding of her fear, while still believing what she did was wrong.

qa.q: Why does understanding Gopika's fear loosen Abhinav's bitterness?
qa.a: Seeing her as a frightened person with a lot at stake makes her human without excusing the act.

qa.q: What might Gopika feel when Abhinav says 'It was still wrong'?
qa.a: Gopika likely feels ashamed but relieved to be spoken to honestly after a year of guilt.

grounding: Stuck on a delayed train, a young man comes to understand the fear behind a friend's betrayal without excusing it, and his bitterness eases.

passage:
Tanuja had not spoken to her older brother Jagdish since he took the gold chain their grandmother left her and pawned it. Six months of silence, even at Diwali.
Then her cousin let something slip at a wedding: Jagdish had lost his job in March and hadn't told anyone. He'd been paying rent with borrowed money and was too ashamed to face their father, who had always called him the failure of the family.
That night Tanuja lay awake. She pictured Jagdish, twenty-three, alone in his rented room in Nagpur, terrified, taking the one thing he knew he could sell. It didn't make it right.
But the anger, which had felt like a hard stone in her chest, softened a little around the edges. He wasn't a villain. He was a scared young man who had made a bad, cowardly choice.
She still didn't call him. Not yet. But she stopped rehearsing the speech about how he'd always been selfish.

qa.q: What did Jagdish take from Tanuja?
qa.a: The gold chain their grandmother left her.

qa.q: What did Tanuja feel lying awake that night?
qa.a: She felt her anger soften a little as she understood her brother's fear and shame, though she still felt wronged.

qa.q: How does Tanuja hold both understanding and the wrong?
qa.a: She sees Jagdish as a scared person without excusing the theft, which loosens bitterness without approving it.

qa.q: What might Jagdish have been feeling when he pawned the chain?
qa.a: Jagdish was likely terrified and ashamed, alone after losing his job and dreading their father's judgement.

grounding: A young woman learns of the fear and shame behind her brother's betrayal and begins to see him as human, without excusing what he did.

"Why did you do it, Jomon?" Sarita asked. They were sitting on the college steps, a year after he had copied her project and submitted it first.
"You want the real answer?"
"I want any answer."
Jomon looked at his hands. "My father said if I failed another semester, I'd be pulled out and sent to work at my uncle's shop. I hadn't slept in days. I saw your file on the shared drive, and I panicked."
"You could have asked me for help."
"I know. I was too proud. Too scared."
Sarita was quiet. She had spent a year imagining him as a smug thief. The boy beside her looked nothing like that. He looked tired, and young, and frightened.
"It was still wrong," she said.
"Completely."
"But I think I understand it a bit now." She felt something in her chest unclench. "That doesn't mean it's okay."
"I know," Jomon said. "Thank you for letting me say it."

qa.q: What did Jomon's father say would happen if he failed?
qa.a: He'd be pulled out and sent to work at his uncle's shop.

qa.q: What did Sarita feel as Jomon explained?
qa.a: She felt something unclench as she saw his fear and exhaustion, while still believing the act was wrong.

qa.q: What does Sarita's 'That doesn't mean it's okay' show?
qa.a: That understanding Jomon's fear is not approval; she can see him as human and still name the wrong.

qa.q: What might Jomon feel being allowed to explain?
qa.a: Jomon likely feels relieved and ashamed, grateful to be heard after a year of guilt.

grounding: A young woman hears the fear behind a classmate's betrayal and understands him more, without excusing what he did.
